description: Solo team. Software engineering student and founder of a small app studio, based in Brazil (UTC-3). Space Apps 2025 Global Nominee. This year I’m going solo on the MODIS and VIIRS hot spots challenge, aiming for a tool that firefighters and civil defense can understand in 30 seconds. Not recruiting teammates, but glad to exchange ideas with other participants. English or Portuguese.
summary: Fire Season Check turns 25 years of NASA FIRMS hotspots from two sensors, MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012), into one consistent weekly record, and answers the question a fire manager already asks: is this season above or below normal? VIIRS counts are put on the MODIS scale (MODIS-equivalent = VIIRS x factor), with a factor fitted per month on each region's own data and tested on years it never saw: typical weekly error 9.2% in Tocantins, Brazil. Through November 1, 2026, Tocantins had 41% fewer hotspots than the average of the previous 10 years, the lowest of 11 years. Firefighters, brigades and civil defence can pick any area and dates inside two validated regions (Tocantins and the Argentine Chaco) and get year-by-week and year-by-month burning calendars, anomalies against the 10-year average and median, CSVs of individual hotspots and images. Our main finding: there is no single MODIS/VIIRS factor; it changes by month, by time of day and by region.
details:
What it does Fire Season Check is a static web page for firefighters, brigade members, civil defence, land managers and scientists. It opens with one sentence and one number: how the current fire season compares with the previous 10 years, and its rank. An explorer lets the user draw a rectangle on a map (or type latitude and longitude) and pick dates. It shows a year-by-week and a year-by-month burning calendar from November 2000, each week and month against the 10-year average and median, the latest month against the median of the same month (October 2026 in Tocantins: -51%), and the busiest month and year in the area. Users can download CSVs (weekly, monthly, per 28 km cell, and every individual hotspot with a harmonized weight) and PNG images of the calendars and the map. Live: https://juniorgcy.github.io/fire-season-check/ (second region: add ?region=chaco).

How it works An offline Python pipeline reads NASA FIRMS archive and near-real-time CSVs (vegetation fires, type 0), merges them without double counting and builds weekly series per sensor. Before 2012 the record is MODIS. After VIIRS starts, it is VIIRS on the MODIS scale: MODIS-equivalent = VIIRS x factor, with one factor per calendar month. The factor is below 1 because VIIRS detects more hotspots than MODIS. It is fitted on the years both satellites fly and scored on years it has not seen (fit 2012-2018, test 2019-2026, and the reverse): median weekly error 9.2% in Tocantins (90th percentile 38.9%) and 9.3% in the Argentine Chaco (33.2%). The answer is recomputed four other ways (MODIS alone, VIIRS alone, fire radiative power, one yearly factor); in Tocantins all give between -38% and -43%. Because the series uses VIIRS after 2012, it keeps going when the ageing MODIS satellites stop.

What we found (creativity) There is no single conversion factor. In Tocantins MODIS sees 0.33 hotspots per VIIRS hotspot in June but 0.21 in October, and 0.27 on daytime passes but 0.19 at night. Over the year the factor is 0.246 in Tocantins but 0.308 in the Argentine Chaco, so a factor copied from one region is about 25% off in the other. The night factor is the same (0.19) in both regions, so the difference comes from daytime passes. A stress test on the Paraná Delta, where fires are small, gave a 23% weekly error, so we left it off the page. There, 2026 looks -60% against the mean but only -8% against the median, because the extreme fires of 2020 and 2022 inflate the mean. This is why the page shows the median next to the mean.

Benefits and intended impact A brigade or civil defence office gets a consistent 25-year picture of its own area in seconds, sees which weeks and months are critical, and compares the current season or month with history, using the same yardstick as the Tocantins state fire plan (the 10-year average). Every number carries its measured error, so users know how much to trust it. The page has no server and no keys, works on a phone, and has loading, error, empty and ready states, accessible colour ramps, keyboard use and text alternatives.

Factors we considered and limits Different pixel sizes, sensitivity and overpass times of MODIS and VIIRS; near-real-time data is provisional (the newest weeks are marked). Two validated regions: the pipeline re-validates any FIRMS box, but two regions are evidence, not proof. One factor for day and night together; VIIRS S-NPP only (not NOAA-20/21). Small areas have larger errors (the page warns). Hotspots are satellite detections, not confirmed fires, and no brigade has field-tested the tool yet.

Next steps Separate day and night factors, NOAA-20/21 VIIRS, more regions with a median-first headline where the mean misleads, and a field test with Tocantins brigades.

Tools Python, pandas, NumPy and pytest (80 automated tests) for the pipeline; HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript for the page; GitHub Pages for hosting. No external JavaScript libraries.

Use of Super Intelligence Built with the help of Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant. The author chose the challenge, chose the approach among the options the assistant listed, chose the users, the regions and how results are shown, and downloaded the NASA FIRMS data. The assistant wrote the code, tests and texts and ran the data checks; the author reviewed the results and decides what is published.
